extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kantian philosophy, metaphysics, and philosophy of religion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for judging physical teleology, moral teleology, and the practical (moral) proof of the existence and attributes of a Supreme Cause (God) as presented in the Critique of the Power of Judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of physical Teleology for Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Teleology (physico-theology) cannot by mere theoretical principles of Reason produce a determinate Theology or a concept of Deity adequate for teleological judging of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical investigation of purposive arrangements can prepare or suggest an intelligent World-Cause, but it cannot reveal whether that Cause has a final design or yield the determinate attributes of a Supreme Being; therefore physico-teleology is only propaedeutic and needs a foreign (practical/moral) principle to become adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for omniscience/omniscience-like knowledge to form a determinate Deity-concept
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a determinate, serviceable theoretical concept of a single intelligent Cause (Deity) one would need omniscience in the judge (to see all purposes and plans) and the power to conceive all possible plans in order to judge the present plan as best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent such theoretical omniscience we cannot derive a determinate idea of the Supreme Cause from experience; claiming otherwise is an overreach of speculative Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between explaining away purposiveness and genuine teleological judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: One may explain apparent teleology as an illusion of Judgement (e.g., by reducing purposiveness to the unity of Substance or mechanism), but such explanation does not resolve the normative question about the ground of purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques that reduce purposiveness to mere mechanistic appearance fail to account for the normative or practical reasons we judge nature teleologically; such reductions are insufficient when assessing teleological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human beings as final purpose in moral Teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is to be an a priori final purpose furnished by Reason, it can be nothing other than man (every rational being) under moral laws; only as moral beings do humans give absolute worth to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating teleological accounts that posit a final purpose, check whether they make rational moral agents the a priori end (rather than mere sentient well-being).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good will as sole ground of absolute worth
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth that makes human existence an absolute final purpose consists in what one does according to the freedom of the faculty of desire — i.e., a good will — and not in cognitive capacity, talents, or happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral-teleological claims by whether they base final worth on moral freedom/good will rather than contingent empirical goods or pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Teleology supplies properties of the Supreme Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: From the principle that humans are final purposes under moral law, we are entitled to think of the First Cause as all-knowing, all-mighty, all-good, and just (properties that together constitute Wisdom), because these are needed for a Cause able to secure the highest good under moral laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical inference: such attributes are ascribed to a Deity insofar as they are conditions for making the moral final purpose practicable, not as empirically established theoretical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof: postulating a moral World-Cause for practicability of final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we cannot represent how happiness and virtue (the components of the highest good) can be brought into harmony by mere natural causes, practical Reason requires postulating a moral World-Cause (God) to render the final purpose possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a practical (not theoretical/apodictic) requirement: the postulate serves the purposive project of moral Reason rather than supplying empirical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summum bonum (highest good) as criterion for final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest good is the combination of the greatest welfare (happiness) of rational beings with the highest condition of good in itself (morality); the moral law prescribes this final purpose a priori as the aim of our practical Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about the final purpose of the world, verify whether they respect this bifurcation: happiness (empirically conditioned) and morality (a priori).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective practical reality vs. objective theoretical reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of a final purpose has subjective practical reality (Reason determines us a priori to promote the summum bonum), but its objective theoretical reality (as part of a speculative explanation of nature) cannot be established by theoretical reflection alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether a claim is being advanced for the practical guidance of action (legitimate in Kant's sense) versus as a theoretical account of nature (not justified by the moral proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative principle of unity of principles (maxim of pure Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining moral and physical teleology by the maxim of pure Reason (seeking unity of principles where possible) gives practical importance to the Idea of God but does not supply speculative cognition of His nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate appeals to unity of principles as a regulative (heuristic/practical) move rather than constitutive theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law does not depend on belief in God
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of the moral law (its unconditional authority) does not depend on the existence of God; the moral law obliges independently, and postulating God is a separate practical postulate to secure the final purpose's possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguments that treat belief in God as the basis or necessary condition of moral obligation in Kant's framework; instead see God as a postulate to reconcile moral aims with the natural order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: moral proof provides practical (reflective) justification only
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral proof establishes a morally-legislating Author sufficiently for the practical use of Reason (reflective judgement), but it does not determine anything theoretically about the actual being or inner constitution of that Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims derived from moral proof should be framed as practical postulates; do not treat them as theoretical knowledge about God's metaphysical nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and anthropomorphism warning in ascribing properties to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Any properties we ascribe to the highest Being must be thought only according to analogy, since we have no similar experience from which to form knowledge of such a Being; thus such ascriptions risk anthropomorphism if taken literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing predicates (e.g., vis locomotiva, omniscience) to God, qualify them as analogical and regulative, not as literal metaphysical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral sentiment as source of the concept of God (distinct from fear-producing gods)
rubrics_metrics.description: While fear produces 'gods' (demons), practical Reason through moral principles can produce the concept of God: gratitude, obedience, and humiliation (moral sentiments) prompt the representation of a morally-legislating Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate motivations for religious concepts: moral disposition yields the concept of a morally-legislating Deity appropriate to Kant's moral proof, whereas fear-based motives yield less robust notions.
